lead: Digital World Acquisition / DWAC — top of the App Store, stuck in line
smaller: Lockheed Martin / LMT — the war trade finally gets its trigger
China Internet ETF / KWEB — the bargain Beijing keeps repricing
3x Nasdaq 100 ETF / TQQQ — the YOLO dip-buy meets a war gap
why_lead: Repeat of the 21 February DWAC lead justified as a material update with newly published launch-day evidence (all 20-21 February): Reuters says Truth Social topped Apple App Store downloads while many users were waitlisted (n1610), Reuters on the app hitting the store (n1603), Forbes on a glitchy start and thousands waitlisted (n1613), Bloomberg on launch-day errors (n1623), CBS on a slow rollout (n1621), Forbes on Hannity and Greene joining (n1618), the Newsweek/PCMag/Business Insider explainer wave (n1614, n1629, n1615), The Independent on a British company's identical-logo legal threat (n1627), The Conversation (n1628), Business Insider's 'peak stupid' professional mood piece (n0788) and Reuters on Wall Street banks' recession fears (n0099). The 21 February lead was a pre-launch buy-the-rumour essay; this one is the post-launch scoreboard-versus-waitlist test going into the first session after Putin's recognition demand (Reuters n0218) and the troop order (Atlantic Council n1137), with a new analog (Coinbase's Super Bowl QR moment, ADWEEK n0080 and the newly published Martin CEO critique n0883) instead of the Virgin Galactic round trip. Recycled 21 February items were dropped in review: the NYT 'crowded field' piece, the ADWEEK 'for whom' piece and the $4.99 rumour fact-check angle. Coinbase led the 15 February edition and appears only as a supporting analog. DWAC still shows its 84.32 USD 18 February close because of Presidents' Day, so Tuesday's open is the first price reaction. Relation to earlier notes: DWAC was a 17 February smaller item ('Truth Social's first screenshot') and the 21 February lead; it was not used 1-16 February.
why_smaller: Lockheed Martin: the war trade gets a new, concrete trigger after the 21 February edition, Putin's call to recognise the breakaway regions (Reuters n0218) and the troop order (Atlantic Council n1137, its characterisation, attributed); card shows LMT 386.46 USD, +4.11% 20s but -2.46% 5s, ITA -0.84% 5s and Rheinmetall -2.70% on 21 February, so the item is about a trade that has not yet worked, with Beijing's renewed Lockheed/Raytheon sanctions (Reuters n0794) as a cross-current. Defense contractors were not used in earlier retail notes (war-hedge items used Exxon on 2 and 8 February, GDX on 14 and 21 February, GLD on 17 February and USO on 15 February; the 21 February notes rejected defense because no war-trade rally had appeared).

China internet ETF (KWEB): replaces the Ford sum-of-the-parts item removed in independent review. A new narrative for the month, the contrarian China-tech bargain: CNBC's investment banks saying it is time to buy Chinese stocks (n0155) and Business Insider on Tencent joining the world's ten most valuable companies as Meta slid (n0561), against Beijing's food-delivery fee order (WSJ n0693; Bloomberg's $26 billion Meituan wipe-out n0694), the US notorious-markets listing (Reuters n0200) and Hillhouse ditching Alibaba (Caixin n0324). Card: KWEB 35.60 USD, -5.04% on 18 February; BABA -4.37%; Tencent 423.03 HKD, -5.23% on 21 February; FB 206.16 USD, -32.00% 20s. Chinese tech was not used in earlier retail notes.

TQQQ: brief carryover (153 words, secondary). TQQQ was a 4 February smaller item ('the leveraged dip-buy snaps back') and the 11 February lead ('the dip-buy meets 7.5% inflation'), and SOXL led on 16 February; this item is cut to a short material update built on newly published 17-21 February evidence (Yahoo Finance's YOLO piece n0825, Fortune n0803, AdvisorHub's leveraged-ETF charge n1587) and a new angle, the holiday gap after Putin's address (TQQQ 50.44 USD, -3.39% 1s, -10.99% 20s; VIX 27.75; DAX -2.07% on 21 February), rather than a rebound call.
considered_not_chosen: Bitcoin and altcoins (BTC 37,075.28 USD -3.53% on 21 February, SOL -8.56%, XRP -9.61%): the only market that traded through Putin's address, used as cross-asset backdrop in the lead rather than another crypto item (Bitcoin led on 8 and 14 February, Coinbase on 15 February, and Bitcoin was a smaller item on 4, 9 and 21 February; Solana was a 2 February smaller item).
Gold and GDX: unchanged US card values since the 21 February item, so no new price evidence to justify a carryover.
Polish banks (PEO -6.75%, MBK -6.00% on 21 February): large own-day drops but a nonretail Poland story with no retail-attention evidence.
DraftKings (-21.62% on 18 February), Roblox, Shopify: no new own-date catalyst after 21 February.
Home Depot (pending 22 February results; Reuters preview n1029): outcome unknown at cutoff and no retail-attention angle.

Ford Motor (n1030, Los Angeles Times on the CEO exploring an EV separation): removed in independent review. The only own-date support is a day-granular 21 February stamp from a US Pacific-time outlet, with no earlier corroborating headline, so the report cannot be shown to precede 00:00 UTC 22 February; Ford was also a 7 February smaller item ('the EV dream at a discount').

Oil/USO (Brent 93.54 USD/bbl, card still at 18 February): the war barrel was a 15 February smaller item and the card has no post-recognition oil price, so the war trade is carried by the defense item instead.

Avoided as possibly after the cutoff or superseded: n1270, n1283, n1292, n1293 (Biden agreeing in principle to a Putin summit, a diplomatic track overtaken by the recognition); no sanctions-tranche or Nord Stream headlines were used because those decisions fall on 22 February. Recycled 21 February evidence (NYT n1606 'crowded field', ADWEEK n0869 'for whom', the $4.99 fact-check n1611) was dropped from the lead.
